item.title: Ultrashort laser pulses offer a new way to probe electrons' quantum geometry
item.description: Researchers at Friedrich Schiller University Jena and the University of Regensburg have developed a method for determining, using light, a quantum property of electrons that has hitherto been difficult to access. The focus is on what is known as Berry curvature—a quantity that describes certain geometric properties of the quantum mechanical states of electrons. The researchers measured it in a layer of the semiconductor tungsten diselenide, just one atomic layer thick, using ultrashort laser pul

item.title: Computational model guides lighting design to improve color discrimination in aging eyes
item.description: Researchers have developed a new computational model that accounts for the effects of aging on our eyes' ability to discriminate color. It could help guide lighting designs that make it easier for older adults to perceive colors while preserving the expected appearance for people with typical color vision.

item.title: Faster molecular simulations identify promising diamond defects for quantum computers and sensors
item.description: A faster way of finding the best diamond-based materials for quantum computers has been developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL). The new approach has already identified promising materials for practical quantum sensors and computers that could one day transform scientific research as a whole. The research was recently published in the journal ACS Central Science and has already garnered attention from other experts in the fiel

item.title: Quantum physicists trace a century of controlling spin
item.description: A concept from the field of quantum mechanics, spin is a property of particles that has no direct counterpart in everyday experience. Since the early 20th century, researchers have learned to manipulate it deliberately by means of precisely shaped electromagnetic pulses. This has resulted in two technologies that are widespread today: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is commonplace in hospitals, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) is used to determine the structures of proteins and

item.title: One step closer to quantum computers that can correct their own mistakes
item.description: Researchers from Rutgers, IBM and collaborating institutions have shown that a quantum computer can check what is happening inside it and respond while it is running, repeatedly resetting parts of the system to bring chaotic behavior under control.

item.title: Hybrid quantum computers could finally get to grips with light and matter
item.description: Many of nature's most important processes depend on how particles of matter interact with light and other force-carrying particles. So far, however, it has proven difficult for conventional computers to determine how individual particles behave in these interactions.

item.title: Ultraviolet laser pulses engineer diamond defects selectively, leaving quantum qubits intact
item.description: When we think about a diamond, we often think about a material whose value comes from its perfection. In my research, however, I am interested in something almost opposite: the tiny imperfections inside diamonds. These atomic-scale defects can give diamonds new optical and electronic properties, and some of them can serve as quantum systems. The challenge is learning how to control these defects without disturbing the others.

item.title: Quantum chip holds multiple photons at once, opening path to scalable memory
item.description: For highly fragile quantum information systems, the ability to store quantum information is vital—but also challenging. Quantum information is transported in particles of light called photons, which often must be temporarily paused (or "stored") while other, slower quantum operations catch up. This storage must be performed on microchips as small as 1 centimeter (0.4 inches)—a distance covered by light in a few trillionths of a second. item.title: Light reads electron spins inside porous crystals, opening path to quantum chemical sensors
item.description: University of Glasgow researchers are part of an international collaboration that could lead to a new generation of quantum sensors. The team, which included researchers from the University of Tokyo, University of Glasgow, University of Sheffield and Kobe University, has for the first time used light to read out the magnetic spin of electrons trapped inside a porous crystalline material known as a metal-organic framework (MOF).

item.title: Ultrafast core-level spectroscopy reveals elusive precursors of exciton condensation in quantum materials
item.description: Many fascinating phases in quantum materials emerge when electrons, atoms and other microscopic components begin to act collectively. But these phases do not necessarily appear out of nowhere when a material crosses a transition temperature. Before long-range order develops, microscopic fluctuations can already be present.

item.title: Physics model reveals fundamental trade-off between prediction and energy efficiency in intelligent systems
item.description: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming part of our everyday lives, from digital assistants to robots that respond to their surroundings. Each of these capabilities is based on physical computational processes that consume energy. An international research team led by Hans Briegel from the Department of Theoretical Physics at the University of Innsbruck, Austria, has investigated the physical limits on the efficiency with which intelligent systems process information. Their findings are

item.title: Quantum 'birthmarks' hold lasting traces of a system's past
item.description: Some classical physical systems can explore many configurations over time until their long-term behavior no longer reveals their starting conditions. The sampling of available configurations according to the appropriate statistical distribution is a property called ergodicity.

item.title: New stability rules distinguish quantum phases of matter that an older method wrongly groups together
item.description: Most of us recognize basic phases of matter and their properties: solids maintain their shape, liquids flow freely with constant volume, and gases expand to fill their container. Quantum phases, on the other hand, are much harder to categorize, overturning traditional notions of what a phase even is and forcing physicists to rethink their definitions.

item.title: Magnetic sculpting transforms single-source fields into predetermined shapes with mathematical precision
item.description: Magnetic fields are invisible yet essential components in technologies ranging from MRI scanners and particle accelerators to atomic clocks and future quantum computers. Each of these applications requires magnetic fields with specific shapes and properties. Today, creating such tailored magnetic fields requires researchers and engineers to design specialized, carefully optimized magnets or large systems of coils for each individual application—a complex and resource-intensive process.

item.title: 诺奖颁给冰立方：“天马行空的想法，值得被支持几十年”
item.description: 2026年10月6日，冰立方中微子天文台（IceCube）项目发起人弗朗西斯·哈尔岑（Francis Halzen）获得诺贝尔物理学奖。

item.title: “冰立方”为何获得2026诺贝尔物理奖？现场对话诺奖评委
item.description: 1988年，弗朗西斯·哈尔岑（Francis Halzen）提出一个构想，利用南极深处的冰层探测来自宇宙的中微子。二十多年后，这一构想成为覆盖一立方公里冰层的冰立方（IceCube）中微子天文台。借助埋在冰中的光传感器，研究人员捕捉到了具有天体物理起源的高能中微子，为研究遥远宇宙中的高能过程提供了新的观测途径。

item.title: 95岁获诺奖的卡根，中国弟子眼中的老师与学者
item.description: “卡根告诉我，好的研究在于质量，而不在于数量。他提到，自己的课题组人数最多时也只有十人左右，很多时候还要更少。后来我经常向同事和学生讲起这件事。在我看来，他所追求的科研理念，就是做新的化学、不一样的化学、有引领性的化学。”

item.title: 95岁卡根终于等到诺奖，25年前法国部长曾为他写信抱不平
item.description: 10月7日，瑞典皇家科学院将2026年诺贝尔化学奖授予法国化学家亨利·卡根（Henri B. Kagan）和硤合宪三（Kenso Soai），表彰他们发现不对称有机合成中的非线性效应和自催化现象。

item.title: 2026诺贝尔化学奖给了法国95岁学者和日本75岁学者，日本科学诺奖得主已有28位
item.description: 10月7日，2026年诺贝尔化学奖授予亨利·卡根（Henri B. Kagan）和硤合宪三（Kenso Soai），以表彰他们“发现不对称有机合成中的非线性效应与自催化现象”。2001年，诺贝尔化学奖表彰不对称催化研究，获奖者为威廉·诺尔斯、野依良治和巴里·夏普莱斯。卡根未获奖，引发法国学界不满，时任法国科研部长致信诺贝尔基金会。《自然》当年报道了这场争议。25年后，95岁的卡根因不对称合成中另一项贡献终获诺奖。

item.title: Optical skyrmions can control the motion of magnetic skyrmions
item.description: Magnetic skyrmions (MSks) are swirling patterns of magnetization that form inside certain magnetic materials. They can behave like actual particles in many ways, exhibiting a stable internal structure and distinct boundaries. Because they are extremely small and can be pushed around with relatively little energy, MSks are regarded as promising information carriers in emerging technologies, including low-power memories and logic circuits. However, a major goal in the field has been to find practi

item.title: 'Carpet' growth method yields long-sought 2D quantum material
item.description: For decades, physicists have sought a practical two-dimensional topological insulator: an ultrathin material whose interior blocks electricity but whose edges conduct it. In ordinary wires, electrons constantly bounce off imperfections, losing energy. But along the edges of a 2D topological insulator, electrons with opposite spins travel in opposite directions, like cars in one-way lanes, so they rarely scatter and lose energy.

item.title: 光遗传学终于获得诺奖
item.description: 2026年10月5日，诺贝尔大会宣布，2026年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖授予卡尔·戴瑟罗斯（Karl Deisseroth）、彼得·黑格曼（Peter Hegemann）和格奥尔格·纳格尔（Georg Nagel），以表彰他们“在光门控离子通道和光遗传学方面的发现”。

item.title: 杨振宁先生在石溪
item.description: 对于杨振宁，中国读者熟悉的，多是他2003年回到清华园之后的岁月；而从1966年至1999年在石溪的33年，是杨振宁一生中最长的一段任职。

item.title: 诺奖得主格拉肖忆杨振宁：“我依然认为他是天才”
item.description: 诺奖得主格拉肖眼中的杨振宁：敢发表“错”论文的天才。

item.title: 尼安德特人和丹尼索瓦人算不算智人?
item.description: 尼安德特人、丹尼索瓦人与现代人的祖先之间存在真实的基因交流，并留下了可育后代。但这究竟意味着他们属于同一物种，还是只是边界模糊的近亲？科学家们给出了截然不同的答案。

item.title: Lensless imaging method enables long-term monitoring of living cells without staining
item.description: In a study led by Tampere University, researchers have developed a new lensless imaging method that produces precise quantitative data on living cells from a single image. The compact system can be placed inside a standard cell-culture incubator, allowing living cells to be monitored continuously for hours or even days without staining or other labels. The research is published in the journal Applied Physics Letters.

item.title: Could consciousness be quantum?
item.description: A controversial idea linking quantum physics and consciousness is moving from speculation towards experiments that could finally put it to the test

item.title: Could meditation reveal an SU(3) symmetry shared by the observer and the universe?
item.description: You sit down to meditate. A conversation returns, then thoughts. You bring your attention back to the breath. Sometimes, after many such returns, the effort eases. Thoughts lose their urgency, while awareness remains clear. Less occupies the mind, yet the moment still feels whole.

item.title: Is ‘Attention’ the Essence of Intelligence?
item.description: A mathematical mechanism enables AI models to process language at scale, undergirding the current AI revolution. Our columnist asks: Why is attention the key? The post Is ‘Attention’ the Essence of Intelligence? first appeared on Quanta Magazine
